Yellow Bellflower originated in New Jersey in the 1700s and takes its name from its distinctive elongated, bell-like shape, tapering from a broad base to a narrower crown, unlike the more rounded shape of most common apples. The pale yellow skin, often blushed with a soft pink flush on the sun-exposed side, covers crisp, juicy, tart flesh that mellows somewhat in storage, making it a genuinely versatile apple good for fresh eating once fully ripe, excellent in pies and sauce for its bright acidity, and historically valued for cider as well. The tree is a reliable, long-lived bearer; harvest in mid to late fall once fruit fully colors, and store cool for good keeping quality through much of the winter.

Black Gilliflower, also historically known as Sheepnose for its distinctive elongated, conical shape said to resemble a sheep's nose, is a New England heirloom dating to the 1700s prized for skin that darkens to a deep, dusky purple-red so intense it appears nearly black, one of the most visually striking older American apple varieties. The dry, mildly sweet, somewhat coarse flesh is not as juicy as many modern apples but was historically valued for baking whole and for its distinctive appearance in mixed heirloom displays. The tree is a dependable, long-lived bearer typical of old New England farmstead varieties; harvest in fall once fruit fully darkens, and expect moderate storage life typical of the era's cooking apples.

Gilpin, also called Little Red Romanite, is a Virginia and Appalachian heirloom famous historically for its extraordinary keeping ability, remaining crisp and usable in cold storage for many months longer than nearly any other common apple variety, a trait that made it invaluable for pre-refrigeration households needing fresh fruit through the depths of winter. The small, deep red fruit has firm, dense, notably tart flesh, sharp fresh off the tree but mellowing somewhat with extended storage, and it was historically prized as a cider apple as much as for eating and cooking. The productive, hardy tree suits mountain and upland Appalachian growing conditions well; harvest in fall once fruit fully colors, and store cool for exceptional long-term keeping.

Buckingham, also historically known as Byers, is a large Southern heirloom apple with red-striped skin over a yellow-green background, carrying juicy, well-balanced sweet-tart flesh that made it a favorite for fresh eating, cooking, and cider across the mid-Atlantic and upper South for generations. The tree is well adapted to warmer Southern growing conditions than many Northern-bred heirlooms tolerate comfortably, making it a good option for gardeners in the middle latitudes of apple-growing range wanting a genuine historic Southern variety. Harvest in fall once fruit fully colors, and expect reasonably good, though not exceptional, storage life in cool conditions.

Milam is a Southern heirloom apple, likely originating in Virginia or North Carolina in the early 1800s, valued historically for a rare combination of drought tolerance, disease resistance, and reliable annual bearing that made it a dependable choice for Southern farmsteads without irrigation or modern spray programs. The small to medium red fruit has crisp, mildly sweet-tart flesh and keeps reasonably well in cool storage, useful for extending fresh apple availability into winter. The tree's genuine toughness and adaptability to less-than-ideal growing conditions have kept it valued among heirloom orchardists in the South even as more demanding, higher-input modern varieties have become common elsewhere. Harvest in fall once fruit fully colors.
